correctness.rationale: The displayed 18-symbol word has a four-position attractor at {0,3,8,13}; a six-factor coverage family has no three-position transversal. For length<=18, distinct positive gaps imply k<=4 and each gap is at most 17; complete ordered-vector enumeration covers exactly 528 cases. An independent implementation from the factor-occurrence and hitting-set definitions checked all 528 words; 156 have gamma=2, 370 gamma=3 and exactly 2 have gamma=4, the stated reversals. This is exhaustive after a proved length bound, not a sampling extrapolation. Computation source verify.py and detailed proof were inspected.

evidence: Increasing-gap theorem gamma=ceil(k/2)+1 covers monotone gap order, whereas exceptional gap sequence (1,3,2,7) is nonmonotone. General factor covering and infinite-word results do not specify this ordered-gap finite threshold.
broader_coverage.reasoning: Permuting gaps changes word factors and attractor number, so the all-increasing theorem does not cover the unrestricted distinct-gap case.

value.rationale: The string-attractor parameter is central to dictionary-compression repetitiveness, and sparse marker words are a natural controlled family; removing the strictly increasing order restriction creates the first genuinely order-dependent four-attractor examples. The sharp cutoff and unique reversal class are concrete, non-implied finite boundary data, without claims about general long strings.
